claims.text: High compressive loading induces local chemical ordering in the initially single-phase, Cantor-like high-entropy alloy.
High strain-rate loading induces incipient secondary-phase formation in the initially single-phase alloy.
Stress-induced ordering or secondary-phase formation impairs dislocation mobility.
Stress-induced ordering or secondary-phase formation reduces activation of multiple nanoscale deformation mechanisms.
Suppression of dislocation mobility and multiple deformation mechanisms reduces ductility and toughness.
The loading-induced microstructural transformation causes a transition from ductile behavior toward brittle fracture.
The initial material is an as-cast, homogeneous, single-phase FCC solid solution similar to CrMnFeCoNi.
Aggressive mechanical loading supplies sufficient energy for atoms to overcome barriers that maintain a metastable random solid solution.
The initial random solid solution is metastable with respect to local ordering or precipitation.
Multiple deformation mechanisms promote high strength, work hardening, and ductility in single-phase CrMnFeCoNi.
Ordering is preferentially produced under high compression rather than tensile loading.
High-compression samples will develop ordered domains relative to low-stress or tensile controls.
High-compression or high-strain-rate samples will develop secondary-phase precipitates relative to the controls.
High-compression or high-strain-rate samples will show lower ductility and toughness than the baseline.
The fracture mode will shift from ductile to brittle under high-compression or high-strain-rate loading.
Low-stress or tensile loading does not induce local ordering or phase separation in the baseline samples.
The proposed behavior applies to shock, cyclic compression, and cyclic impact at room to moderately elevated temperatures.
The absence of both loading-induced ordering or phase transformation and any change in toughness or fracture mode would falsify the hypothesis.
